rows.speaker: traditional accounts
rows.claim: Traditional accounts describe ʿĀʾishah twice losing her necklace; the first search led to the revelation on dry ablution, while the later search preceded the slander episode.
rows.anchor: According to the traditional accounts, while on a journey ʿĀʾishah’s necklace fell from her neck two times.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣafwān found ʿĀʾishah and returned her; sources describe him as valorous and chaste, tending the Prophet’s camel in battles and dying in battle under ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: Ṣafwān is described in the sources as having been a valorous, chaste man who tended the Prophet’s camel during battles and was later killed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusers were usually identified as Ḥassān ibn Thābit, Misṭaḥ ibn Uthāthah, and Ḥamnah bint Jaḥsh; other accounts put the group at ten to forty.
rows.anchor: mainly of three people,ḥassān ibn Thābit, Misṭaḥ ibn Uthāthah, and Ḥamnah bint Jaḥsh

rows.speaker: other reports
rows.claim: Alternative reports say the group involved ten or as many as forty people.
rows.anchor: others report that the group consisted of ten or even up to forty persons

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The person who undertook the greater part is commonly identified as Ḥassān, understood as the rumor's initiator and therefore most blameworthy.
rows.anchor: refer to Ḥassān ibn Thābit; this phrase is meant to refer to the person who began the rumor

rows.speaker: some reports
rows.claim: Some reports say Ḥassān later went blind, which some interpreted as recompense for his role.
rows.anchor: According to some reports, Ḥassān later went blind, which was interpreted by some as his recompense

rows.speaker: reports
rows.claim: Other accounts record Ṣafwān striking Ḥassān on the head with his sword, but not lethally.
rows.anchor: Ṣafwān struck a nonlethal blow to his head with his sword

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others identify the person who undertook most of the slander as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy, the hypocrites' leader who played a major role.
rows.anchor: Others interpret the one who undertook the greater part of it to refer to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports differ on corporal punishment: one says only Ḥassān was punished, others say all three main accusers, and others say none for lack of clear evidence.
rows.anchor: There are also differing reports as to whether the Prophet beat or lashed these three scandalmongers.

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī compares the gap between moral guilt and criminal liability here to the Quran's frequent mention of hypocrites without naming them so as to ground a legal claim.
rows.anchor:
For al-
Qurṭubī this gap between moral culpability and criminal liability is reminiscent of the fact

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī reports the best-known account as saying the three were lashed, while ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy was not.
rows.anchor: in the most well known account these three were lashed, but thatʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy was not

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lie's exposure benefited the community by openly resolving uncertainty and putting the affair to rest.
rows.anchor: either because, rather than leaving the people suspicious and uncertain, the matter was resolved openly and put to rest

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the scandal occasioned Quranic verses that clarified the matter.
rows.anchor: or because it resulted in the revelation of these Quranic verses about the issue

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the false accusers, the episode could stop continued sin or impose worldly punishment that would avert a harsher punishment hereafter.
rows.anchor: preventing them from carrying on in sin or as providing a punishment in this life that would avert a harsher punishment in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers should resist suspicion and avoid repeating claims whose source is unreliable or unknown.
rows.anchor: the ethical principle of erring against suspicion and not repeating something one has heard if its source is unreliable or unknown

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī cites a hadith likening Muslims to one body: injury to one part afflicts the whole with fever and sleeplessness.
rows.anchor: al-Rāzī quotes the ḥadīth, “In their togetherness and compassion for one another and what God placed between them, the Muslims are like unto a single body.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Positive presumption means assuming other people innocent and of good character; toward God it means trusting in divine compassion and mercy.
rows.anchor: In the former case, it refers to the presumption of innocence and good character in others, and in relation to God it refers to belief in God’s Compassion and Mercy.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accusations of sexual misconduct require four eyewitnesses, as also stated in 4:15 and 24:4.
rows.anchor: the requirement that accusations of sexual misconduct be supported by four eyewitnesses

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says an accuser may be truthful yet, without four witnesses, must be treated legally as a liar regardless of the claim's merits.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī discusses the possibility that a person might be truthful in his or her accusation of adultery, but fail to produce four witnesses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran often condemns empty or useless talk, including in 4:140, 6:68, and 9:65.
rows.anchor: Empty or vain talk about subjects without benefit is a vice frequently condemned in the Quran

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The phrase literally means meeting the lie with one's tongues: people readily received and transmitted it.
rows.anchor: meaning that they received and transmitted the lie readily

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read talaqqawna as taliqūna, from a different root, yielding senses of penetrating like a weapon or acting and following quickly; the phrase can mean spreading the lie quickly.
rows.anchor: some read as taliqūna (from

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the matter slight means the speakers thought no sin would attach to it.
rows.anchor: Slight is understood to mean that they thought no sin would attach to them on its account

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gossip and backbiting are grave vices even when the statement is true; see also 49:12.
rows.anchor: In traditional Islamic ethics gossip and backbiting are considered serious vices, even when what is being said is true

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Buhtān means backbiting through lies, distinguished from damaging backbiting that recounts something factually true.
rows.anchor: buhtān, which signifies backbiting by telling lies (Q), since one can also backbite by relating that which is factually true but still damaging

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Glory be to Thee may express astonishment at the calumny.
rows.anchor: is understood as an expression of astonishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the exclamation implicitly declares that the wife of God's chosen Messenger could not have done this.
rows.anchor: an implicit declaration that the wife of God’s chosen Messenger could not do such a thing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it declares that God is too glorious to leave the matter unattended.
rows.anchor: an exclamation that God is too Glorious to leave this matter unattended

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī cites hadiths on calumny, including that a Muslim is one from whose tongue Muslims are safe and an emigrant leaves what God forbids.
rows.anchor: al-Rāzī mentions several aḥādīth pertaining to it, such as, “A Muslim is he from whose tongue the Muslims are safe

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: If you are believers means the accusers should heed God's exhortation and never repeat this kind of accusation.
rows.anchor: Exhortation(Ṭ) and never repeat the same type of accusation

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: God's signs here can mean laws and rulings that benefit His servants.
rows.anchor: in this case the signs can be understood as referring to the laws and rulings that benefit His servants

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase God makes clear the signs also appears in 2:187, 2:221, 2:242, 3:103, 5:89, and 24:59.
rows.anchor: God makes clear the signs is mentioned elsewhere in the Quran

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Those who want indecency spread among believers face punishment unless they sincerely repent.
rows.anchor: Those who desire that indecency be spread among believers shall be punished unless they make sincere repentance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This passage warns against slander-mongering and reminds believers that God knows their inner thoughts.
rows.anchor: this entire passage, is understood as a warning against such slander-mongering and a reminder to the believers that their inner thoughts are not hidden from God

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr cites a hadith against insulting believers or seeking their faults: God will expose those who search out a Muslim brother's faults.
rows.anchor: Ibn Kathīr mentions the ḥadīth, “Do not insult the servants of God, and do not reproach them, and do not look for their faults.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The result of the conditional phrase were it not is left implicit, as it is in verse 10.
rows.anchor: The result contingent upon were it not is implied (cf. v. 10)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without God's bounty, slanderers would fare worse through ultimate perdition or because the slander spread farther; the clause may also anticipate verse 21's point about purification.
rows.anchor: either through their own ultimate perdition or because the slander would have spread even farther

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers are told not to follow Satan's steps, which lead to indecency and wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: Other verses that mention following in the footsteps of Satan include

words: وَمَن يَتَّبِعْ خُطُوَٰتِ ٱلشَّيْطَٰنِ فَإِنَّهُۥ يَأْمُرُ بِٱلْفَحْشَآءِ وَٱلْمُنكَرِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran elsewhere says Satan commands evil or indecency, in 2:169 and 2:268.
rows.anchor: That Satan commands to evil or indecency is also mentioned in

words: مَا زَكَىٰ مِنكُم مِّنْ أَحَدٍ أَبَدًۭا
rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q glosses being purified as becoming upright or righteous, ṣāliḥ.
rows.anchor: To be pure is understood here to mean to be upright or righteous (ṣāliḥ; Q)

words: مَا زَكَىٰ مِنكُم مِّنْ أَحَدٍ أَبَدًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reported interpretation takes purity to mean being rightly guided.
rows.anchor: or to be rightly guided

words: مَا زَكَىٰ مِنكُم مِّنْ أَحَدٍ أَبَدًۭا
rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ reports that purity here can mean following Islam.
rows.anchor: or to follow Islam (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some connect the verse to Abū Bakr, who gave charity to his impoverished maternal cousin Misṭaḥ until learning that he had spread the lie about ʿĀʾishah, then vowed to stop.
rows.anchor: Some connect this verse to Abū Bakr, who used to give charity to his impoverished maternal cousin, Misṭaḥ ibn Uthāthah.

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Other commentators say the verse concerns all such people, rather than only Abū Bakr and Misṭaḥ.
rows.anchor: Others say this verse was revealed in connection with all such persons

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: After the verse, Abū Bakr said he wanted God's forgiveness, resumed charity to Misṭaḥ, and vowed not to withhold it.
rows.anchor: after this verse was revealed, Abū Bakr said, “Yea, by God I desire, O Lord, that Thou forgivest us!” returned to Miṣtaḥ

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some call this the Quran's most hopeful verse because it shows God's kindness even to people who slander.
rows.anchor: Some commentators speak of this verse as the “most hopeful” in the Quran, as it shows God’s Kindness even to those who commit slander

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī notes the moral challenge to Abū Bakr: continue giving charity to the man who defamed his daughter, answering evil with good.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī notes the great moral challenge that this verse presented to Abū Bakr

words: فِى بُيُوتٍ أَذِنَ ٱللَّهُ أَن تُرْفَعَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is usually read as continuing the previous verse, with the niche's lamp located within houses.
rows.anchor: This verse is usually read as a continuation of the previous verse, meaning that the lamp or “lighted wick” is in a niche within houses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One continuation reading takes the light to be kindled in the houses.
rows.anchor: or, similarly, that the light is kindled in the houses

words: فِى بُيُوتٍ أَذِنَ ٱللَّهُ أَن تُرْفَعَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase begins a new sentence: God permits houses to be raised and His Name remembered there, where He is glorified morning and evening.
rows.anchor: It could also be read as a new sentence: “In houses that God has permitted to be raised and wherein His Name is remembered

rows.speaker: many
rows.claim: Many commentators understand the houses to be mosques.
rows.anchor: By houses many understand mosques

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others extend houses to mean all houses.
rows.anchor: while others extend it to mean all houses

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Other interpretations specify the Kaʿbah, Jerusalem's Holy Sanctuary, the Prophet's mosque in Madinah, or Qubāʾ mosque.
rows.anchor: or else specific places such as the Kaʿbah, the Holy Sanctuary (in Jerusalem), the Prophet’s mosque in Madinah, or the Qubāʾ mosque

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raising the houses can mean their construction, their exaltation, or both.
rows.anchor: That the houses are raised refers to either the building of such houses, their exaltation, or both

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators take glorification here to refer to the canonical Muslim prayer, ṣalāh.
rows.anchor: refers to the Muslim canonical prayer(ṣalāh

rows.speaker: Sufis
rows.claim: Sufis read houses symbolically as human hearts illuminated by the remembrance of God's Name.
rows.anchor: houses is understood here by Sufis to be a symbol for the illumination of the hearts of human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The juxtaposition of houses and remembrance evokes 22:40's list of monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques where God's Name is much mentioned.
rows.anchor: The juxtaposition of the general word houses and the remembrance of God’s Name is also suggestive of the different kinds of houses of worship mentioned in

words: لَّا تُلْهِيهِمْ تِجَٰرَةٌۭ وَلَا بَيْعٌ عَن ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording parallels 63:9's warning not to let property or children divert from God's remembrance and 62:9's command to leave trade for Friday prayer.
rows.anchor: The language here is similar to that in 63:9: Let neither your property nor your children divert you from the remembrance of God; and 62:9

words: يَخَافُونَ يَوْمًۭا تَتَقَلَّبُ فِيهِ ٱلْقُلُوبُ وَٱلْأَبْصَٰرُ
rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The turning about of eyes and hearts refers to the terror and awe of Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: The phrase when eyes and hearts will be turned about refers to the terror and awe experienced on the Day of Judgment

words: يَخَافُونَ يَوْمًۭا تَتَقَلَّبُ فِيهِ ٱلْقُلُوبُ وَٱلْأَبْصَٰرُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imagery recalls 14:42–43, where eyes stare transfixed and hearts are vacant on the Day of Judgment.
rows.anchor: related imagery is used to describe eyes and hearts in 14:42–43

rows.speaker: Sufis
rows.claim: Continuing the symbolism, houses can represent the hearts of people who fear being turned away from God's remembrance.
rows.anchor: the houses can be said to symbolize the hearts of those who are afraid of their eyes and hearts being turned away from the remembrance of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For God's sovereignty, the commentary points to Sūrah 67, 67:1, and 36:83.
rows.anchor: For God’s sovereignty, see Sūrah 67, “Sovereignty”; see also 67:1c; 36:83c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rejection of God's having a child addresses Arab pagan claims of divine daughters and the Christian doctrine of Jesus as God's son.
rows.anchor: the notion of God having a child, which includes both Arab pagan beliefs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Measured it out translates qaddara followed by its cognate verbal noun taqdīr.
rows.anchor: and the verb’s corresponding verbal noun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taqdīr includes both knowing a thing's measure and bestowing a measure, with senses of estimation and ordainment.
rows.anchor: encompasses both knowing the measure of a thing and bestowing a measure upon a thing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term bears on created order, God's knowledge and power, and thus divine omniscience and omnipotence.
rows.anchor: implications for the theological questions surrounding the order found in creation as well as both God’s Knowledge of things and His Power over them

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī distinguishes human taqdīr as estimation from God's eternal, unchanging knowledge of each creature's whole existence from beginning to end.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī notes that, as it concerns human beings, taqdīr is an act of estimation or assessment

rows.speaker: IK and Q
rows.claim: Other commentators stress taqdīr as ordainment or predestination of all that a creature was, is, or will be; it resembles qadar, one's allotted measure and the doctrine of predestination.
rows.anchor: Other commentators emphasize the sense of taqdīr as ordainment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran was revealed across the Prophet's mission over twenty-two or twenty-three years.
rows.anchor: The Quran was revealed over the course of the Prophet’s entire mission of twenty-two or twenty-three years

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise to strengthen the Prophet's heart echoes 11:120, which says accounts of earlier messengers strengthen it.
rows.anchor: The message of this verse is connected with 11:120: All that We recount unto thee of the stories of the messengers is that whereby We make firm thine heart

rows.speaker: IK and Ṭ
rows.claim: Some understand the measured recitation to mean that God explained the Quran's interpretation to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: Some understand We have recited it unto thee in a measured pace to mean, “We have explained to thee its interpretation”

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Gradual revelation tracked the Prophet's life, legislated commands and prohibitions over time, helped establish the community, and supported him in struggles with enemies.
rows.anchor: the relationship of the Quran to the events of the life of the Prophet, the gradual legislation of commands and prohibitions

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī lists benefits of successive revelation: gradual legislation, learning and memorizing in portions, and responses suited to believers' questions and circumstances.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī understands the gradual application of the commands and prohibitions, the memorization and understanding of one part at a time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The divided recitation also connects to 17:106, which describes reciting the Quran to people in intervals through successive revelation.
rows.anchor: see also commentary on 17:106: And [We sent it down] as a recitation We have divided in parts

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some say the Quran first descended all at once from the Preserved Tablet or Mother of the Book to the lowest heaven, then descended gradually to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: some commentators describe how the Quran descended all at once from the Preserved Tablet (85:22) or Mother of the Book (13:39)

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some cite the proverb that sleep is the brother of death when explaining waking as resurrection.
rows.anchor: some mention the proverb, “Sleep is the brother of death”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sleep is associated with death in 6:60 and 39:42, which says God takes souls both at death and during sleep.
rows.anchor: Sleep is also associated with death in 6:60: He it is Who takes your souls by night, and also 39:42

words: ٱلَّيْلَ لِبَاسًۭا وَٱلنَّوْمَ سُبَاتًۭا وَجَعَلَ ٱلنَّهَارَ نُشُورًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night, sleep, and day are described in similar language in 78:9–11.
rows.anchor: The night, sleep, and day are described using similar language in 78:9–11.

rows.claim: The exchange recalls 20:91, where Israelites tell Aaron they will remain devoted to their idol, and 20:97, where Moses confronts them about that devotion.
